titre: Homicide and Offspring: Yanomami and Waorani Compared
accroche: In 1988, Chagnon links homicide and offspring among the Yanomami. In 2009, a study of the Waorani does not find this link.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1988, the journal Science published an article by Napoleon Chagnon drawn from 23 years of study among the Yanomami of Amazonas, Venezuela. He derives figures from it: 44% of men estimated to be 25 or older had taken part in the killing of someone; about 30% of adult male deaths are due to violence; nearly 70% of adults estimated to be over 40 had lost a close genetic relative this way. According to the abstract, men who have killed have more wives and more children than those who have not.

## Who Is “One Who Has Killed”

Chagnon works with a local category, the unokai: men who underwent a purification rite after taking part in a homicide. The article argues that revenge, kinship, and warfare are linked, and that reproductive variables must enter explanations of tribal violence. It also puts forward, cautiously, that cultural success can lead to biological success. According to Beckerman and his coauthors, a good share of the critical responses attributed a stronger thesis to him: that selection would favor genes for aggressiveness. These same authors note that the article elicited an unusual number of responses, from field specialists and outside commentators alike.

## Another Warrior People

In 2009, Stephen Beckerman and colleagues published in PNAS a study of the Waorani of Ecuador, who may have the highest homicide rate of any society known to anthropology. They interviewed 121 elders of both sexes about genealogies and about the raids in which they or their relatives had taken part, and reconstructed the complete histories of 95 warriors.

To avoid certain methodological objections raised against Chagnon, their sample includes living men and dead men, and aggressiveness is measured by the number of raids a man took part in, not by a local word whose meaning is contested.

The result does not confirm the Yanomami model. Among the Waorani, the most ardent warriors, however defined, do not obtain more wives, do not have more children, and their wives and children do not live longer. The statistically clearest difference even runs the other way: belligerent men have fewer children who reach the age of 15. The authors caution that some calculations rest on only 3 to 7 individuals, with low statistical power.

## What the Gap Allows Us to Say

Beckerman and his coauthors specify that their study is not an evaluation of Chagnon's model as such, nor a simple replication among another people. They offer one lead for the gap between these two South American warrior societies: the spacing of revenge raids.

What this changes: the link between violence and offspring observed among the Yanomami is not a rule that would hold for every warrior society, since another people with a very high rate of violence does not show it. Why, the authors do not settle. A question of measurement also remains: a ritual status like unokai and a tally of raids may not designate the same men.

repere.texte: Among the Yanomami, 44% of men estimated to be 25 or older had taken part in the killing of someone, and about 30% of adult male deaths are due to violence (Chagnon, Science, 1988, abstract).
repere.source: Napoleon A. Chagnon, “Life histories, blood revenge, and warfare in a tribal population,” Science, 239 (4843), 1988, pp. 985-992

carte.punch: Among the Yanomami, men who have killed have more children. Among the Waorani, no such link.
carte.idee: Chagnon (1988) reports that Yanomami who took part in a homicide have more wives and children. Beckerman et al. (2009) interview 121 Waorani: their most aggressive warriors have no more descendants, and fewer who reach the age of 15.

quiz.question: How does the 2009 study of the Waorani differ from Chagnon's study of the Yanomami?
choix: Their most aggressive warriors have no more children, and have fewer who reach the age of 15
The Waorani did not carry out revenge raids, unlike the Yanomami according to Chagnon
The Waorani killed far less than the Yanomami, which was enough to explain the gap
The Waorani were not asked about their children, only about their marriages and their raids
quiz.explication: Among the Waorani, the most ardent warriors have neither more wives nor more children, and the clearest difference is that they have fewer children who reach the age of 15. The authors study precisely their revenge raids and estimate that the homicide rate there may be the highest known; children and marriages are indeed part of their data.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Chagnon's article published in 1988, what proportion of Yanomami men estimated to be 25 or older had taken part in the killing of someone?
choix: 70% of adults estimated to be over 40
44% of men estimated to be 25 or older
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1988 article puts at 44% the men aged 25 or older who had taken part in the killing of someone; the 30% concerns adult male deaths due to violence, and the 70% concerns adults over 40 who had lost a close genetic relative this way.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is an unokai, in the sense in which Chagnon uses the term in 1988?
choix: A man who underwent a purification rite after taking part in a homicide
A man who lost a close genetic relative to violence
A raid leader in charge of organizing revenge between lineages
A term for women married to several warriors
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Chagnon works with this local category: the unokai are men who underwent a purification rite after taking part in a homicide, not the victims, the raid organizers, or a female status.

quiz_supplementaire.question: To avoid certain methodological objections raised against Chagnon's study, how do Beckerman and his coauthors measure the aggressiveness of Waorani warriors in 2009?
choix: By unokai status, as among the Yanomami
By the number of raids a man took part in, and not by a contested local term
By the number of children who reached the age of 15
By the direct testimony of only the 95 warriors still living
quiz_supplementaire.explication: To avoid the objections raised against Chagnon, Beckerman and his coauthors measure aggressiveness by the number of raids, not by a local term with a contested meaning such as unokai; their sample also includes living men and dead men, not just the living.
